meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Trichophyton mentagrophytes

Trichophyton mentagrophytes is specifically noted as being transmitted from rodents to man among the classified zoophilic dermatophytes.

Correct Option Explanation

In contrast, T. verrucosum is transmitted from cattle and horses, while Microsporum canis comes from dogs and cats.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Trichophyton verrucosum instead is transmitted from cattle and horses to man, not rodents.
  • Microsporum canis is transmitted from dogs and cats to man, not rodents.
  • Trichophyton schoenleinii causes Favus (crusted ringworm), not specifically linked to rodent transmission here.
Know More
  • Zoophilic dermatophytes specifically infect animals.
  • Geophilic dermatophytes are saprophytes from soil.
  • T. simii is commonly distributed in India.
  • The classic pattern in animal hair infection is called ectothrix.

posts.post_content: Prior to and after administering anthrax spore vaccine to animals, for how many days should antibiotics be withheld?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 2 to 3 days

Antibiotics should not be administered for 2 to 3 days before and after anthrax spore vaccination in animals.

Correct Option Explanation

This precaution ensures the live spore vaccine can establish adequate immunity without antibiotic interference.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Same day only understates the actual precautionary window recommended.
  • 7 days overstates the specific precautionary window given in the source.
  • 14 days considerably overstates the specific precautionary window given in the source.
Know More
  • Pregnant animals should not be vaccinated against anthrax.
  • Stern's vaccine (spore vaccine) was developed in 1939.
  • Anthrax carcasses should never be opened.
  • Burial pits for anthrax carcasses should be 2 meters deep.

posts.post_content: Rift Valley fever and West Nile fever are cited as examples of which specific mode of vector-borne zoonotic transmission, where the pathogen passes from one generation of vector to the next?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Trans-ovarian transmission

Rift Valley fever and West Nile fever are cited as examples of trans-ovarian transmission, where the pathogen passes through the vector's eggs to the next generation.

Correct Option Explanation

This mode of transmission allows the vector population itself to serve as a reservoir, sustaining the pathogen even without an external vertebrate host.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Propagative transmission instead involves the agent multiplying within the vector before host injection, exemplified by plague and yellow fever.
  • Developmental transmission instead involves the agent merely developing (not multiplying) in the vector, exemplified by Dirofilaria immitis.
  • Cyclo-propagative transmission involves both development and multiplication, exemplified by Trypanosoma cruzi in bugs.
Know More
  • Propagative transmission is exemplified by plague and yellow fever.
  • Developmental transmission is exemplified by Dirofilaria immitis.
  • Cyclo-propagative transmission is exemplified by Trypanosoma cruzi.
  • Tick-borne encephalitis also involves trans-ovarian transmission (metazoonosis subtype IV).

posts.post_content: Chronic Q fever, particularly with endocarditis in persons with pre-existing valvular disease, can have a case fatality rate as high as what percentage?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 60%

Chronic Q fever, especially with endocarditis in persons with pre-existing valvular disease, can have a case fatality rate as high as 60%.

Correct Option Explanation

This contrasts sharply with the acute form of Q fever, which typically has a low mortality rate of about 1%, except when endocarditis is present.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • 10% considerably understates the actual documented chronic Q fever fatality rate.
  • 25% also understates the actual documented fatality rate.
  • 40% still understates the documented 60% figure for chronic Q fever fatality.
Know More
  • Acute Q fever mortality is usually low, about 1%.
  • Chronic Q fever requires prolonged antibiotic treatment, sometimes years.
  • Q fever gives a negative Weil-Felix test.
  • The tick vector is Ixodes ricinus.
